stem: A client with opioid-induced respiratory depression improves after naloxone. Which nursing action is most important after the initial response?

options.A: Continue close surveillance for recurrent opioid effects and be prepared to repeat naloxone as clinically necessary because some opioids can outlast naloxone.
options.B: End close surveillance once respirations and alertness normalize after the first dose because a satisfactory response means opioid depression will not recur.
options.C: Give additional naloxone at fixed intervals even if respiratory depression does not recur because repeat dosing is required after every initial response.
options.D: Focus follow-up monitoring on withdrawal symptoms rather than recurrent respiratory depression because naloxone provides longer action than most opioids.

rationale: Current DailyMed labeling states that a patient who responds satisfactorily to naloxone should remain under continued surveillance and that repeated naloxone doses should be administered as necessary because the duration of action of some opioids may exceed that of naloxone. Therefore A is correct. B stops monitoring despite the labeled recurrence risk. C incorrectly converts repeat dosing from clinically necessary to a fixed schedule. D reverses the duration relationship and neglects the possibility of recurrent opioid-induced respiratory depression.
educational_objective: After an initial response to naloxone, continue surveillance for recurrent opioid effects and be prepared to repeat naloxone when clinically necessary because some opioids can outlast naloxone.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine
source_document_title: Naloxone Hydrochloride Injection, USP — Prescribing Information
source_locator: Warnings > Repeat Administration and Dosage and Administration: a patient who has satisfactorily responded to naloxone should be kept under continued surveillance and repeated doses should be administered as necessary because the duration of action of some opioids may exceed that of naloxone.
source_claim_supported: After an initial satisfactory response to naloxone, continued surveillance is required and repeat dosing may be necessary because opioid effects can recur after naloxone wears off.

correction_summary: Removed the absolute-word cue and rebuilt all four choices to be length-balanced, clinically plausible post-naloxone management decisions.

audit_findings.stem: PASS — focused on the clinically important period after an initial naloxone response.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly matches current labeling and is uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — falsely assumes recurrence cannot occur after an initial satisfactory response.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — repeat naloxone is given as necessary, not automatically on a fixed schedule when recurrent opioid effects are absent.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — reverses the duration relationship and under-monitors recurrent respiratory depression.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that preserves both continued surveillance and clinically indicated repeat dosing.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B stops monitoring, C mandates unnecessary scheduled redosing, and D neglects recurrent opioid effects.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — no absolute-word cue remains and option lengths are closely matched.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies directly covers medication-response evaluation and intervention after adverse effects.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether repeat naloxone should be automatic after every response; current labeling explicitly says repeated doses are administered as necessary, confirming A and excluding C.
